blocks.text: ONO-02 · Transliteration and variants
Lesson overview

⁧مُحَمَّد⁩ you can find written Muḥammad, Muhammad, Mohammed, Mohammad, Mohamed; ⁧يُوسُف⁩ becomes Yusuf, Youssef, Yousef, Youcef. They are not mistakes: every country and every European language has its own habits, and none is official for all. In this unit you learn the most common Latin spellings (English, French, Egyptian), their reasons, and above all the method of going back from Latin to Arabic: what Arabic letters can be behind a Latin letter, where are the ambiguities, when you have to ask. You also learn to spell a name in Arabic. A week.

rows: ONO-01 exceeded; name of the letters (L0)
6–7 hours · one week (week 71 of the calendar)

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Anki deck A2 (Tag ONO-02), script for speech synthesis, session with tutor
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. explain why the same name has many Latin spells;
2. read the most common English, French and Egyptian spellings and connect them to Arabic letters;
3. Reduce a Latin spelling to the possible Arabic forms, recognizing ambiguities (Hassan: ⁧حَسَن⁩ or ⁧حَسَّان⁩ ?);
4. recognizing the Arabizi of messages (3 = ⁧ع⁩ , 7 = ⁧ح⁩ );
5. spell a name in Arabic and understand a spelling dictation.

2. Why so many graphs
1. There is no single system. Scholars use precise systems with diacritical signs (in this DIN course
31635: Muḥammad, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān); documents and everyday life use simple, unmarked graphs.

2. Two European traditions. In the countries related to English (Golfo, Iraq, Jordan, Egypt in part) it is written "English" (sh, j, oo, ee); in the countries related to French (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Lebanon in part) (ch, dj, ou).
3. The local pronunciation. Each transcribes as he says: the Egyptian says Gamāl and writes Gamal; correspondent in the Maghreb short vowels often fall (Mohamed, Fatma).
4. The papers. The machine-readable part of the passport (the two lines at the bottom, with the marks <) uses only capital Latin letters without marks: no apostrophes, no accents, no ʿ.
5. Personal choice. Many people choose their own handwriting and keep it, even if it does not follow No rules.

5. National traditions
The table indicates frequent habits, not rules: an Egyptian can write Mohammed and a Moroccan Muhammad.
6. The Arabic of Messages
Many Arabic speakers write Arabic (often the dialect) in Latin letters in messages and social media, using figures for sounds that the Latin alphabet does not have. The most common:
Other figures (6, 8, 9) and variants with the apostrophe (3' = ⁧غ⁩ , 7' = ⁧خ⁩ ) change from country to country. The arabizi must be recognized: it is not a handwriting to use in documents.
7. From Latin to Arabic: the method
1. Island the consonants and ask what Arabic letters can stand behind each (Table 3 and table below).
2. Look for the name among those you know: the Arab names frequent are a few hundred. Hassan with each probability is ⁧حَسَن⁩ or ⁧حَسَّان⁩ ; Tarek is ⁧طَارِق⁩ , ⁧تارك⁩ .
3. Look at the origin of the handwriting: ou, ch, dj suggest French; g per ⁧ج⁩ Egypt; ee, oo English.
4. Lists all possibilities when they remain ambiguity, without choosing at random.
5. Ask: The safest thing is to have the person write the name in Arabic, or read it in the Arabic part of the document. Ambiguous Latin letters.
Frequent ambiguity.
8. The name in documents
• In Arabic passports the name appears in Arabic and Latin characters: the Arabic form is the reference.
• The same person may have different Latin graphs in different documents (passport, permission to Stay, college card): write down all the graphs you find and the Arabic form.
• In the machine-readable part of the passport, the surname is first followed by < < and the name; spaces and Thicknesses become <. A name like ⁧عَبْد الرَّحْمٰن⁩ can appear divided into two words.
• When you write an Arabic name in Latin letters (in a minutes, in a list), use the document's spelling of the person, not yours.

10. Pronunciation

The couples that the Latin spelling confuses must be pronounced well when you ask: ḥāʾ / hāʾ (Ḥasan is not "Hasan" with light sucked h), sīn / ṣād, tāʾ / ṭāʾ, dāl / ḍād. ʿayn. ʿĀʾiša, ʿAlī, ʿAbd: ʿ is pronounced even if the Latin spelling does not write it. ǧīm. In standard Arabic it is pronounced [dʒ] as in "Giro": Ǧamāl. The pronunciation [g] is from Cairo: recognize it, but do not use it in the standard.
